theme: At the set time I will judge with equity
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 75. It is a short psalm in which God speaks about his appointed time to judge. Notice how the psalm moves between praise, a divine oracle, and the psalmist’s response.
settingTheScene: Psalm 75 is a psalm of Asaph, set to the tune “Do Not Destroy.” It likely belongs to the time of the Assyrian crisis. The people are surrounded by arrogant powers, and the question is when God will act. The answer comes in a divine oracle: God has an appointed time, and he will judge with equity. It is a good companion to the oracles against the nations you have just read.
observation: “We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near” (v. 1).
“At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity” (v. 2).
“When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars” (v. 3).
“I say to the boastful, Do not boast, and to the wicked, Do not lift up your horn” (v. 4).
“Do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck” (v. 5).
“For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up” (v. 6).
“But it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another” (v. 7).
“All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with thanks. The strange thing is that the thanks come before the judgment. The psalmist is confident that God is near, and he can give thanks in advance. This is the posture of faith. We thank God not only for what he has done but for what he is going to do.

Then God speaks: “At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity.” Two things are stressed. First, God has a schedule. Judgment is not rushed or delayed by accident. It will come at the right moment, when he decides. People often think that because judgment is delayed, it will never come. The psalm says it will. Second, God judges with equity. He does not act capriciously. His judgment is perfectly fair.

When the earth totters and the foundations seem to shake, God says it is he who steadies its pillars. In the Assyrian crisis, with kingdoms collapsing, the world seemed unstable. The psalm assures us that the stability of the world rests on God.

Then the oracle addresses the arrogant: do not boast, do not lift up your horn. The horn is a symbol of strength and pride. The proud think they can raise themselves. But “not from the east or from the west… comes lifting up.” No human direction offers promotion. “It is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another.” Everything depends on him.

The cup in verse 8 is a cup of wrath. The wicked of the earth will drink it to the dregs. Against that, the psalmist says: “I will declare it forever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.” The final verse contrasts the horns of the wicked, which will be cut off, with the horns of the righteous, which will be lifted up.
connection: Mary’s song says, “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52). Jesus said that those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted (Luke 14:11). 1 Peter 5:6 says, “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you.” Jesus drank the cup of God’s wrath on the cross (Mark 14:36).
application:
If you are tempted to boast, remember that all lifting up comes from God.

If you are waiting for justice, trust God’s set time, and give thanks in advance.

Pray for stability for those whose world is shaking.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God for being near.
Ask him to keep you from boasting.
Thank him that he judges with equity.
